pos: n. (one of the two gods of Sepharvaim to whom the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire; also the name of a son of Sennacherib who murdered his father in the house of Nisroch)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Adrammelek, apparently Adar is king or the glory of the king, compounding a deity name with melek, king. The -melech element runs through the whole family of these names — Molech, Milcom, Malcham, Anammelech — and every one of them attaches kingship to a false god.
biblical_def: Adrammelech is named in the passage that explains how the religion of Samaria came to be what it was. When Assyria deported Israel, the king “brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel” (2Ki 17:24), and each transplanted people carried its gods along: “Howbeit every nation made gods of their own, and put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made” (2Ki 17:29). Then comes the inventory, and the worst of it: “And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim” (2Ki 17:31). Human sacrifice, and of one's own children, was the settled worship of the people the empire moved into the land God had emptied for that very sin. A second Adrammelech in Scripture is a son of Sennacherib: as the Assyrian king “was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword” (2Ki 19:37) — a king murdered by his own children in his own temple, the exact judgment the god of that name was fed with.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Adrammelech; in sacred history he is one of the gods of Sepharvaim, to whom children were burnt in the fire, and the name of a parricide son of Sennacherib.
webster_full: ADRAMMELECH, n. An idol of the Sepharvites, planted by the Assyrians in the cities of Samaria.
The name signifies the glory or magnificence of the king.
The Sepharvites burnt their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech.
A son of Sennacherib king of Assyria bore the same name.
He and his brother Sharezer slew their father as he worshipped in the house of Nisroch.
scriptures: And the king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel: and they possessed Samaria, and dwelt in the cities thereof.
Howbeit every nation made gods of their own, and put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made, every nation in their cities wherein they dwelt.
And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.

And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead.
corruption_summary: Ancient child sacrifice is filed away as a barbarism of the distant past, and the modern practice of destroying children for the sake of one's own future is not connected to it. Scripture names the act by what it is and treats the god behind it as the constant.
corruption_paragraphs: The comfortable modern reading is that the Sepharvites belonged to a cruel and superstitious age, and that our own civilisation, whatever its faults, has left such things behind. It has not. The essential logic of the fire has never gone away: a child is destroyed so that the parent may obtain prosperity, security, standing, or relief. That is what the worshippers of Adrammelech were buying, and it is what a culture that destroys the unborn in the millions is buying — with anaesthetic instead of drums, and a clinical vocabulary instead of a priest, but for the same consideration. The dictionary declines to describe the ancient practice as barbarism and the present one as a matter of policy.

God's word on the subject is not measured. He calls it the thing He hates: “for every abomination to the LORD, which he hateth, have they done unto their gods; for even their sons and their daughters they have burnt in the fire to their gods” (Deu 12:31), and He forbids Israel to pass any of their seed through the fire to Molech (Lev 18:21). He also declares what children are: “Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward” (Psa 127:3). And He announces the end of the god who eats them, along with every other: the idols He shall utterly abolish. The name Adrammelech survives only because Scripture wrote down what was done in it.

pos: n. (the second of the two gods of Sepharvaim, named with Adrammelech as receiving the children of the Sepharvites in the fire)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Anammelek, compounding Anu or Anah, a Mesopotamian deity name, with melek, king — hence Anu is king. Like its companion, the name is a claim of sovereignty, and the claim was honoured with the lives of children.
biblical_def: Anammelech appears once in Scripture, in the same clause as Adrammelech: “the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim” (2Ki 17:31). The chapter that contains it is the great post-mortem on the northern kingdom. Israel had been carried away for doing precisely what the imported nations then did in the same hills, and the writer sets out the newcomers' religion with a cold precision: Succothbenoth of Babylon, Nergal of Cuth, Ashima of Hamath, Nibhaz and Tartak of the Avites, Adrammelech and Anammelech of Sepharvaim. Then he gives the verdict that names the disease exactly: “They feared the LORD, and served their own gods, after the manner of the nations whom they carried away from thence” (2Ki 17:33). Not apostasy outright — something more durable. They added the LORD to a shelf that already had seven gods on it, and the arrangement lasted: “So these nations feared the LORD, and served their graven images, both their children, and their children's children: as did their fathers, so do they unto this day” (2Ki 17:41). That is the origin of the Samaritan religion the Lord speaks of at Jacob's well.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Anammelech; in sacred history he is a god of the Sepharvites, worshipped in the cities of Samaria with the burning of children.
webster_full: ANAMMELECH, n. An idol of the men of Sepharvaim, named with Adrammelech.
The name is compounded with melech, a king, as are several of the heathen deities.
The Sepharvites, planted in Samaria by the king of Assyria, burnt their children to these gods.
The nations so planted feared the LORD and served their own gods together.
So did their children and their children's children, as the sacred writer records.

And the men of Babylon made Succothbenoth, and the men of Cuth made Nergal, and the men of Hamath made Ashima,
corruption_summary: Syncretism is now commended as religious generosity and called by softer names — interfaith respect, multiple paths, honouring every tradition. Second Kings 17 gives it its exact description: they feared the LORD and served their own gods, and God did not accept the arrangement.
corruption_paragraphs: The men resettled in Samaria were not atheists and were not hostile to the God of Israel. They sent for a priest, learned the manner of the God of the land, and added Him to their worship with genuine seriousness. By every modern standard of religious tolerance they behaved well. The Holy Ghost's summary of their piety is one sentence long: they feared the LORD, and served their own gods. That is the biblical definition of syncretism, and it is the form idolatry takes in a pluralist society, which is why the verse matters more now than it did in the age of open paganism.

The first commandment does not read thou shalt have me among thy gods. It reads, “Thou shalt have no other gods before me” (Exo 20:3), and the LORD gives His reason as a personal one: “for thou shalt worship no other god: for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God” (Exo 34:14). Christ made the same demand absolute: “No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24), and “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6). A church that presents Christ as one valid path among several has not become gracious. It has become Samaria, and Samaria burned children.

pos: n. (the idol or sacred object made by the men of Babylon after their settlement in the cities of Samaria)
etymology: From Hebrew Sukkoth Benoth, literally booths of daughters — sukkah, a booth or tabernacle, with bath, a daughter. The name has been explained as the tents in which Babylonian women were prostituted in the service of their goddess, and as a Hebrew rendering of a Babylonian divine title; the older expositors generally took the first.
biblical_def: Succothbenoth heads the list of the gods of the resettled nations: “And the men of Babylon made Succothbenoth, and the men of Cuth made Nergal, and the men of Hamath made Ashima” (2Ki 17:30). The name is unlike the others in the list, which are ordinary divine names; this one is a Hebrew phrase — booths of daughters — and it reads as a description rather than a title. If the common explanation is right, the men of Babylon set up in Samaria the shrine-booths in which women were given to strangers as an act of worship, a practice the Greek historians describe of Babylon and which the prophets denounce wherever Israel imitated it. Whether the phrase names a structure or a goddess, the setting is fixed by the chapter: this was introduced into the land the LORD had just emptied, into “the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made” (2Ki 17:29), and it was practised alongside a professed fear of the LORD (2Ki 17:33). Israel had been sent into captivity for exactly this — the high places, the groves, the whoredom under every green tree — and the replacement population began doing it before the deportation ships were unloaded.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Succothbenoth; in sacred history it is the idol or sacred booth made by the men of Babylon in the cities of Samaria.
webster_full: SUCCOTHBENOTH, n. The booths of daughters; an object of worship set up in Samaria.
It was made by the men of Babylon, whom the king of Assyria planted in the land.
The name is understood by many of the tents wherein women were prostituted to the idol.
Others take it for a Hebrew form of a Babylonian divine title.
It stands first in the list of the gods which the transplanted nations made for themselves.

corruption_summary: Ritual prostitution is treated as an exotic feature of ancient religion with no modern counterpart. Scripture treats sexual sin and idolatry as one subject throughout, and the pairing is exactly as live now as it was in Samaria.
corruption_paragraphs: It is usual to read the sacred prostitution of the ancient world as a curiosity — a religious form so alien that it tells us nothing about ourselves. Scripture makes no such separation. The prophets use the same vocabulary for both sins because they are the same sin looked at from two sides: Israel goes a whoring after other gods, and Israel goes a whoring in the ordinary sense, and Hosea was told to marry a wife of whoredoms to make the point unmissable. Where a false god is worshipped, the body follows; where the body is given away, a god is being served.

Paul reasons in precisely this way to a Gentile church in a city famous for its temple women. He rehearses Israel's wilderness sins — “Neither be ye idolaters, as were some of them” (1Co 10:7), “Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed” (1Co 10:8) — as one connected warning, and he names covetousness itself as idolatry (Col 3:5). The booths of daughters have not disappeared from the world; they have been rebuilt as an industry, and the worship they serve is the same. The answer Paul gives is not a strategy but a fact of ownership: “For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God&#39;s” (1Co 6:20).

pos: n. (the god made by the men of Cuth when they were planted in the cities of Samaria; a Babylonian deity of war and the underworld)
etymology: From Hebrew Nergal, taken over from the Babylonian; the name is generally understood as the great man or the great hero, and in the Mesopotamian religion it belonged to the god of war, plague and the realm of the dead. The element survives in the name of Nebuchadnezzar's officer Nergalsharezer, who sat in the middle gate when Jerusalem fell (Jer 39:3).
biblical_def: Nergal is named once as an object of worship: “the men of Cuth made Nergal” (2Ki 17:30), in the list of the gods the Assyrian resettlement brought into Samaria. The men of Cuth gave their name to the whole population — the Jews of the second temple period called the Samaritans Cuthites — so the god of that particular contingent has a certain grim prominence in the story. What he was in his own country is worth knowing: the Mesopotamian Nergal presided over war, pestilence and the underworld, a deity of death whose favour was sought by men who feared him. That is the ordinary shape of paganism. The gods of the nations are powers to be appeased, and the worshipper's hope is to be overlooked. The chapter that names him is a chapter about death: a kingdom destroyed for idolatry, its people deported, its land restocked, and the newcomers importing a death-god into the vacancy while professing to fear the LORD (2Ki 17:33). The element appears again at the fall of Jerusalem, in the name of a Babylonian prince: “Nergalsharezer, Samgarnebo, Sarsechim, Rabsaris, Nergalsharezer, Rabmag” (Jer 39:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Nergal; in sacred history he is the god of the men of Cuth, set up in the cities of Samaria.
webster_full: NERGAL, n. An idol of the men of Cuth, or Cuthah, in the cities of Samaria.

The men of Cuth were planted in Samaria by the king of Assyria.
The element of the name appears in Nergalsharezer, a prince of Babylon at the taking of Jerusalem.

corruption_summary: Comparative religion presents the gods of the nations as parallel expressions of a common human search, differing from Israel's faith only in style. Scripture calls them nothing, and then calls them devils, and holds both statements at once.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard academic treatment sets Nergal beside the LORD as two entries in a catalogue of ancient near eastern deities, with Israel's monotheism explained as a late development out of the same soil. The Bible refuses the shelf. Its first word about the idols is that they are nothing at all: “They that make a graven image are all of them vanity; and their delectable things shall not profit” (Isa 44:9), and “They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not” (Psa 115:5). An idol is a manufactured object with nobody behind it, and the man who prays to it is talking to wood.

Its second word is that something real is nevertheless being served. Paul holds both together in one passage without embarrassment: “we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one” (1Co 8:4), and then, of the same sacrifices, “the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God” (1Co 10:20). Nergal was not a rival deity; there is no such thing. He was a name over an emptiness, and behind the emptiness a real spiritual power taking the worship. That is why Scripture never treats paganism as harmless error, and why it never treats an idol as a competitor either.

pos: n. (the god made by the men of Hamath when they were settled in the cities of Samaria)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Ashiyma', of uncertain derivation; it is close in form to 'asham, guilt or a trespass offering, which the older expositors did not fail to notice. The god of the men of Hamath bears, in Hebrew ears, a name that sounds like guilt.
biblical_def: Ashima is named once: “the men of Hamath made Ashima” (2Ki 17:30). Hamath was a Syrian city on the Orontes, taken by Assyria in the same campaigns that swallowed Israel, and its people were among those the king planted in Samaria to hold the country. Nothing is told of the god's form or worship. What the verse supplies is the pattern — each nation made its own gods, put them in the high places of a land that had been judged for high places, and settled down. Amos had already named Hamath in his warning to the careless rich of Samaria: “Pass ye unto Calneh, and see; and from thence go ye to Hamath the great: then go down to Gath of the Philistines: be they better than these kingdoms?” (Amo 6:2). The great cities the northern kingdom envied and imitated were carried away, and their gods were then carried into the hills of Ephraim by men who would in time be told at a well in Sychar: “Ye worship ye know not what: we know what we worship: for salvation is of the Jews” (Joh 4:22).

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that a nation which admires and imitates the great powers around it will end by importing their gods, and that Amos said so before it happened.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Ashima is a Syrian idol named once and nobody has contested it. What the sequence of events sets before the reader is a warning about cultural admiration. Amos rebukes the notables of Samaria for looking at Calneh and Hamath and Gath — the impressive kingdoms of the day — and taking their measure from them, lying on beds of ivory and putting far away the evil day. Within a generation Hamath had fallen, Samaria had fallen, and the gods of Hamath were standing in Samaria's shrines.

The principle to recover is that a church takes on the character of whatever it admires. Israel wanted a king like all the nations, and got one; the northern kingdom wanted the sophistication of Damascus and Hamath, and got their idols. The New Testament states the law of it directly: “And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Rom 12:2), and John warns that the love of the world and the love of the Father cannot occupy the same heart (1Jn 2:15). Congregations rarely resolve to adopt the world's gods. They admire the world's success first, and the gods arrive with the furniture.

pos: n. (one of the two gods made by the Avites when the king of Assyria planted them in the cities of Samaria)
etymology: From Hebrew Nibchaz, of unknown derivation; the older lexicographers connected it with a root meaning to bark, and the rabbinical tradition accordingly figured the idol with the form of a dog. Nothing in Scripture describes it, and the dictionary reports the tradition without adopting it.
biblical_def: Nibhaz appears in one clause with its companion: “And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak” (2Ki 17:31). The Avites came from Ava, one of the places the king of Assyria emptied to fill Samaria: “the king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim” (2Ki 17:24). Ava appears again in Rabshakeh's taunt under the walls of Jerusalem, in the list of cities whose gods had failed to save them — “Where are the gods of Hamath, and of Arpad? where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah?” (2Ki 18:34) — and Hezekiah's answer in the temple is the theology of this whole subject in two sentences: those were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone, and therefore they were destroyed. The Avites carried Nibhaz to Samaria anyway. Men do not abandon a god because it has been proved powerless; they carry it into exile with them, and their children keep it (2Ki 17:41).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Nibhaz; in sacred history it is an idol of the Avites, set up in the cities of Samaria.
webster_full: NIBHAZ, n. An idol of the Avites, who were planted in Samaria by the king of Assyria.
It is named with Tartak, the other god of that people.
The Scriptures describe neither its form nor the manner of its worship.
The Jewish writers have supposed the figure to have been that of a dog.
Ava, whence the Avites came, is named by Rabshakeh among the cities whose gods could not deliver them.

Where are the gods of Hamath, and of Arpad? where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah? have they delivered Samaria out of mine hand?
And have cast their gods into the fire: for they were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone: therefore they have destroyed them.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that an idol demonstrably unable to save is not thereby abandoned, because idolatry is not a mistake of the intellect but a disposition of the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nibhaz is an unexplained idol named once and nobody has contested it. What the story around it exposes is the strange durability of a discredited god. The Avites had watched their city fall and their gods do nothing; Rabshakeh could use their name as a taunt precisely because everyone knew the record. They packed Nibhaz and took him to Samaria. This is not stupidity. It is the biblical doctrine of the human heart, which does not arrive at its gods by evidence and does not leave them by evidence either.

Hezekiah's prayer states the truth the Avites could not act on: the kings of Assyria destroyed those nations and their gods, “For they were no gods, but the work of men&#39;s hands, wood and stone: therefore they have destroyed them” (2Ki 19:18). Paul explains why the argument does not persuade: men hold the truth in unrighteousness, and having known God, glorified Him not as God, but became vain in their imaginations — “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom 1:22). Which is why the answer to idolatry is not better evidence but a new heart, promised in the same chapter of Ezekiel that describes cleansing from all idols: a new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.

“Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah?” — a taunt built on their failure.
“They were no gods, but the work of men's hands” — Hezekiah's verdict in the temple.

pos: n. (the second of the two gods made by the Avites in the cities of Samaria)
etymology: From Hebrew Tartaq, of unknown derivation. Like Nibhaz its companion, the name has attracted a good deal of rabbinical and antiquarian speculation as to the form of the idol; Scripture supplies none of it, and the dictionary declines to supply it either.
biblical_def: Tartak is named exactly once, in the middle of the inventory of Samaria's imported religion: “And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim” (2Ki 17:31). Nothing else is known of him from the sacred text, and that silence is itself the entry's subject. The writer of Kings is not interested in describing pagan worship; he lists the gods, states what was done in their service where it bears on the judgment, and moves to his verdict. He will spend a chapter on the reason Israel was carried away — they walked in the statutes of the heathen, built high places in all their cities, set up images and groves in every high hill, burned incense in all the high places, wrought wicked things to provoke the LORD to anger — and he will spend one clause on Tartak. The proportion is deliberate. Scripture is a book about the LORD, and it names the idols only far enough to condemn them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Tartak; in sacred history it is an idol of the Avites in the cities of Samaria, named with Nibhaz.
webster_full: TARTAK, n. An idol of the Avites, set up by them in the cities of Samaria.
It is named in the same verse with Nibhaz, the other god of that people.
The sacred writer says nothing of its figure or of the manner of its worship.
The Avites were brought from Ava by the king of Assyria and planted in the land.
Their descendants feared the LORD and served their graven images together.
scriptures: And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.

And the children of Israel did secretly those things that were not right against the LORD their God, and they built them high places in all their cities, from the tower of the watchmen to the fenced city.
And there they burnt incense in all the high places, as did the heathen whom the LORD carried away before them; and wrought wicked things to provoke the LORD to anger:
So these nations feared the LORD, and served their graven images, both their children, and their children's children: as did their fathers, so do they unto this day.
corruption_summary: Modern retellings of the Old Testament frequently spend more attention on the religions of Canaan and Assyria than the Bible does, treating them as the interesting background. Scripture's own proportion is the model: name the idol, condemn it, and preach the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a whole genre of teaching that explains the Old Testament chiefly by the pagan religions surrounding it — the fertility rites, the storm gods, the mythologies of the neighbours — until the Scripture becomes a footnote to the archaeology and the sermon becomes a lecture. Second Kings 17 has every occasion to do this and does not. Seven gods are named in two verses, with a single detail of practice attached to the one that required children, and then the writer returns to his subject: what the LORD had commanded, what Israel had done, and why the land was empty.

The principle is one of preaching more than of scholarship. Paul in Athens is the pattern: he had observed the altars and could quote their poets, and he used one inscription as a doorway — and then he spoke for the rest of the sermon about God who made the world and all things therein, and about repentance, and about the man whom He hath ordained, and about the resurrection (Act 17:22-31). He determined among the Corinthians “not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1Co 2:2). Tartak gets one clause in the Bible. A ministry that gives the idols more room than that has let the background become the picture.

pos: n. (the god of Sennacherib, in whose house the king of Assyria was murdered by his own sons)
etymology: From Hebrew Nisrok, of disputed derivation; some have connected it with nesher, an eagle, and others with an Assyrian divine name. Scripture calls him simply Nisroch his god, and it is the possessive that carries the weight.
biblical_def: Nisroch is named twice, in two parallel accounts of the same night, and both times the sentence is one of the most quietly devastating in the historical books. Sennacherib had stood before Jerusalem and sent word that the God of Hezekiah could no more deliver the city than the gods of Hamath and Sepharvaim had delivered theirs. The angel of the LORD went out and smote the camp; the king departed, and dwelt at Nineveh; and then: “And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead” (2Ki 19:37). Isaiah records it in the same words (Isa 37:38). The man who had asked “Who are they among all the gods of the countries, that have delivered their country out of mine hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of mine hand?” (2Ki 18:35) died at the feet of his own god, killed by his own children, in the one place on earth where he had a right to expect protection. Isaiah had given the whole outcome in advance: “Behold, I will send a blast upon him, and he shall hear a rumour, and return to his own land; and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land” (Isa 37:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Nisroch; in sacred history he is the god of Sennacherib king of Assyria, in whose temple the king was slain by his sons.
webster_full: NISROCH, n. The god of Sennacherib, worshipped at Nineveh.
Some derive the name from the Hebrew word for an eagle.
Sennacherib was worshipping in the house of Nisroch when he was slain.
Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword and escaped into Armenia.
Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead, as the prophet Isaiah had foretold.
scriptures: And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead.

And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword; and they escaped into the land of Armenia: and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead.
Who are they among all the gods of the countries, that have delivered their country out of mine hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of mine hand?
Isa 37:7
Behold, I will send a blast upon him, and he shall hear a rumour, and return to his own land; and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land.
corruption_summary: Sennacherib's death is often narrated purely as an Assyrian palace coup with the biblical framing set aside as pious commentary. Scripture presents it as the prophesied answer of the LORD to a blasphemy spoken against His name, and gives the prophecy before the event.
corruption_paragraphs: Assyrian sources record the assassination, and the modern account of it stops there: a succession dispute, a murdered king, a son on the throne. The biblical writers know the same facts and place them inside a stated cause. Rabshakeh had ranked the LORD with the gods of Hamath and Arpad; Hezekiah spread the letter before the LORD and prayed that all the kingdoms of the earth might know that He alone is God; Isaiah returned the answer, naming three things — a rumour that would turn the king home, a fall by the sword, and his own land as the place of it. All three happened. To call the connection pious commentary is not a historical judgment but a decision about what may be admitted as a cause.

The doctrine is the LORD's jealousy for His own name. He says of the Assyrian's boast, “Because thy rage against me, and thy tumult, is come up into mine ears, therefore will I put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips” (Isa 37:29), and of His glory, “I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8). Sennacherib's last recorded act was worship, and it did not help him. The scene is the plainest illustration in Scripture of the difference between a god a man carries and the God who carries a man.

pos: n. (a heathen deity for whom Ezekiel saw women weeping at the north gate of the LORD's house, in the vision of the abominations of Jerusalem)
etymology: From Hebrew Tammuz, taken from the Babylonian; in Mesopotamian religion the name belonged to a god of vegetation whose annual death and supposed return were mourned and then celebrated in a summer festival. The fourth month of the later Jewish calendar came to bear the name.
biblical_def: Tammuz appears once, in the second of the four escalating abominations Ezekiel is shown in the vision of chapter 8. The prophet is carried in visions of God to Jerusalem and led through a series of doors, each opening on something worse than the last: the image of jealousy at the gate; seventy elders of Israel in a chamber of imagery with censers in their hands, saying the LORD seeth us not; then this: “Then he brought me to the door of the gate of the LORD'S house which was toward the north; and, behold, there sat women weeping for Tammuz” (Eze 8:14). And last, five and twenty men between the porch and the altar with their backs toward the temple and their faces toward the east, worshipping the sun. The Babylonian rite of mourning a dying-and-rising vegetation god was being performed by daughters of Israel in the gate of the house of the living God, and the LORD's comment moves the reader on before the reader is ready: “Hast thou seen this, O son of man? turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations than these” (Eze 8:15). The vision ends with the glory of the LORD departing from the threshold, and the city given to the men with the slaughter weapons.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Tammuz; in sacred history it is a heathen deity for whom women wept at the gate of the temple in Ezekiel's vision.
webster_full: TAMMUZ, n. A deity of the Babylonians, mourned with an annual lamentation.
Ezekiel saw women sitting and weeping for Tammuz at the north gate of the LORD's house.
This was the second of the abominations shewn to the prophet in his vision of Jerusalem.
The rite was borrowed from the heathen and practised within the very courts of the temple.
The fourth month of the later Jewish year bore the name of Tammuz.
scriptures: Eze 8:14
Then he brought me to the door of the gate of the LORD'S house which was toward the north; and, behold, there sat women weeping for Tammuz.
Eze 8:15
Then said he unto me, Hast thou seen this, O son of man? turn thee yet again, and thou shalt see greater abominations than these.
Eze 8:16

And he brought me into the inner court of the LORD'S house, and, behold, at the door of the temple of the LORD, between the porch and the altar, were about five and twenty men, with their backs toward the temple of the LORD, and their faces toward the east; and they worshipped the sun toward the east.
Eze 8:12

Then said he unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth.
corruption_summary: The dying-and-rising god of the nations is routinely offered as the template for the resurrection of Christ. Ezekiel 8 shows Israel mourning such a god as an abomination, and the New Testament rests the resurrection on witnesses, an empty tomb and a datable public event.
corruption_paragraphs: Since the nineteenth century it has been a commonplace of comparative religion that Christianity took its central claim from the vegetation myths — Tammuz, Adonis, Osiris — whose deaths and returns were enacted with the turning of the year. The comparison collapses on inspection. Those cults celebrate a cycle: the god dies and revives every year, in step with the seed and the harvest, and no one supposed there had been a particular week in which it happened or a particular person to whom it happened. The apostolic preaching is the opposite in kind. It names a governor, a date, a city, a tomb, and a list of witnesses, most of them still living when the list was published: Christ died for our sins, was buried, rose again the third day, “After that, he was seen of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present” (1Co 15:6).

Paul also makes plain that nothing symbolic will do. “And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain” (1Co 15:14), and he calls himself a false witness of God if it did not happen. A myth cannot be falsified and does not need to be true; the gospel invites exactly that test. And Ezekiel supplies the church's judgment on the myths themselves: women weeping for Tammuz in the gate of the temple was not an early form of Christian devotion. It was one of the abominations for which the glory departed.

pos: n. (the god of the children of Ammon, called the abomination of the Ammonites, for whom Solomon went aside in his old age; written also Malcham, and closely allied to Molech)
etymology: From Hebrew Milkom, from melek, king, with a suffix — their king. Malcham in Zephaniah is the same word, and Molech is the same root vocalised differently. The Authorized Version keeps the several forms, and the translators' care is worth noting: at 1 Kings 11:5 the Ammonite god is Milcom, and two verses later at 11:7 the abomination Solomon built a high place for is Molech.
biblical_def: Milcom enters at the saddest turn in the history of the monarchy. “For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites” (1Ki 11:5) — the wisest man who ever lived, in his old age, turned aside by his wives to the gods of the nations round about. The LORD's indictment names the same gods: “they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon” (1Ki 11:33), and the kingdom was torn from his son for it. The high places he built stood on the hill before Jerusalem for three hundred years, through every reform, until Josiah: “the high places that were before Jerusalem, which were on the right hand of the mount of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had builded for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Zidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of the Moabites, and for Milcom the abomination of the children of Ammon, did the king defile” (2Ki 23:13). Zephaniah names the god in his roll of those to be cut off, in the form Malcham, and beside him the men who hedge: “them that worship and that swear by the LORD, and that swear by Malcham” (Zep 1:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Milcom; in sacred history he is the god of the Ammonites, called their abomination, worshipped by Solomon in his old age.
webster_full: MILCOM, n. Their king; the god of the children of Ammon.
The name is from the same root with Molech and with Malcham in Zephaniah.
Solomon went after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites, being turned aside by his wives.
He built high places for these gods on the hill that is before Jerusalem.
Josiah defiled those high places, which had stood since the days of Solomon.
scriptures: For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.

Because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon, and have not walked in my ways, to do that which is right in mine eyes, and to keep my statutes and my judgments, as did David his father.

And the high places that were before Jerusalem, which were on the right hand of the mount of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had builded for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Zidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of the Moabites, and for Milcom the abomination of the children of Ammon, did the king defile.
Zep 1:5
And them that worship the host of heaven upon the housetops; and them that worship and that swear by the LORD, and that swear by Malcham;
corruption_summary: Solomon's idolatry is commonly excused as a diplomatic necessity of the ancient world, and his marriages as ordinary statecraft. Scripture treats them as apostasy, names the cause as the unequal yoke, and takes a kingdom away for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The apologetic runs that Solomon's foreign marriages were treaties, that shrines for his wives' gods were a diplomatic courtesy, and that no personal defection need be inferred. The text says he went after Milcom. It says his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father. It says the LORD was angry with Solomon because his heart was turned from the LORD which had appeared unto him twice. The narrative is not describing a policy; it is describing a man, and it takes ten tribes off his son.

The law had stated the mechanism in advance, and the reason for it: a king must not multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away (Deu 17:17), and Israel must not intermarry with the nations, “For they will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other gods” (Deu 7:4). Paul repeats the principle for the church: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness?” (2Co 6:14). And the pattern of the fall is worth naming exactly, because it is the ordinary one: not a sudden renunciation, but an old man's accommodations, made one at a time, each defensible in isolation, on a hill in full view of the temple he had built.
